Heart Murmurs in a Child

innocent vs pathologic murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo · louder on standing · the continuous murmur by locationIs any single feature pathologic, and does the murmur get louder or softer on standing?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • An innocent murmur is grade 1 to 2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory and softer on standing or Valsalva, in a well child with normal vitals, first and second heart sounds (S1, S2), pulses and growth: reassure.
  • Any single pathologic feature (grade 3 or higher, holosystolic or diastolic, harsh, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, symptoms) calls for an electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography.
  • A systolic murmur louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports.

Innocent murmurs are mildly turbulent flow through a normal heart; a diastolic murmur is never innocent. The one benign continuous murmur, the venous hum, disappears supine or with head flexion.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Murmur louder on standing in an athlete, or syncope on exertionHold sports; obtain ECG and echocardiography: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common cause of sudden death in young athletes.
Weak femoral pulses with arm hypertensionCoarctation: measure four-extremity pressures and obtain echocardiography.
Infant with poor weight gain, feeding difficulty or breathing fastHeart failure from a shunt: obtain echocardiography.
Central cyanosis with a murmurCyanotic heart disease: obtain echocardiography.
3Differential
Innocent murmurs
MurmurDecides itNext best step
Still murmurOften ages 2 to 6: vibratory or musical, left lower sternal border; louder supine, softer standing.Reassure.
Pulmonary flow murmurAny age: soft ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border; normal, moving S2.Reassure.
Venous humOften ages 3 to 8: continuous, above the right clavicle; gone supine or with head flexion.Reassure.
Peripheral pulmonary stenosisUnder 1 year: grade 1 or 2 ejection murmur spreading to the axillae and back.Reassure if well; it should be gone by age 1. The American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) advises echocardiography or considering cardiology referral for any newborn murmur, even when well, because structural lesions are more prevalent at that age.
Pathologic murmurs
LesionDecides itNext best step
Holosystolic, left lower sternal border; small is loud and harsh, large tends to be softer.Obtain echocardiography.
Ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border with a wide, fixed split S2.Obtain echocardiography.
Continuous, machine-like, loudest just below the medial end of the left clavicle; congenital rubella.Obtain echocardiography.
Arm hypertension, weak femoral pulses; a systolic or continuous murmur between the shoulder blades on the back.Measure four-extremity pressures; obtain echocardiography.
Pulmonary valve stenosisEjection murmur at the upper left sternal border spreading to the back; ejection click; S2 widely split but moving.Obtain echocardiography.
Aortic stenosisEjection murmur at the upper right sternal border spreading to the carotids.Obtain echocardiography.
Harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border, louder standing or with Valsalva, softer squatting or with handgrip; fourth heart sound (S4); family history of sudden death.Hold sports; obtain ECG and echocardiography. A transient hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from myocardial fat and glycogen deposition resolves by age 1; beta-blockers if symptomatic.
4Workup
Innocent or pathologic: the screening exam
AxisInnocentPathologic
HistoryAsymptomatic, normal growthInfant: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, fast breathing; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance
MurmurEarly or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1 to 2, softer uprightHolosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade 3 or higher, louder or persistent upright
Other findingsNormal vitals, normal S1 and S2, symmetric pulsesCentral cyanosis; loud, fixed or single S2; weak femoral pulses; hepatomegaly
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
A new soft murmur on day 3 after a normal birth examinationA shunt as pulmonary resistance falls, or peripheral pulmonary stenosisCheck where it spreads.
Loudest in the axilla, spreading to the lung fieldsPeripheral pulmonary stenosisReassure if well; confirm it is gone by age 1.
Saturation 99% with normal pulsesAgainst cyanotic disease and coarctationCheck the murmur grade and where it spreads.
S2 split that moves with breathingExcludes an atrial septal defect, whose split is fixedKeep atrial septal defect off the list.

Pause point. Reassurance needs every benign feature; one pathologic feature is enough to order ECG and echocardiography.

Practice
  1. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing → Still murmur → reassurance
  2. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography before sports
  3. 6 yo F, continuous infraclavicular hum that disappears with neck rotation → Venous hum → reassurance
  4. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well → ECG and echocardiography → one pathologic feature is enough
  5. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back → Aortic coarctation → collateral flow murmur
  6. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 → Pulmonic flow murmur → innocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer
  7. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur under the right clavicle that fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine → Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veins → venous hum, and why it is usually right-sided
  8. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture → Patent ductus arteriosus → echocardiography
  9. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses → Coarctation with intercostal collateral flow → echocardiography and four-extremity pressures
  10. 6-week-old with a large ventricular septal defect and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload → Left atrium → left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return
  11. 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure → Patent ductus arteriosus → the machine-like continuous murmur, with a wide pulse pressure
  12. 6 d old M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% → A large ventricular septal defect → soft because a wide defect creates little turbulence
  13. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses → Peripheral pulmonary stenosis → an innocent murmur of the first year
  14. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum below the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down → Venous hum → the one benign murmur that increases upright
  15. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left → The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical → more turbulent flow into the superior vena cava
  16. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms → Echocardiography → peripheral pulmonary stenosis belongs to the first year
  17. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses → Reassurance → the full benign profile is present
  18. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat → Hold sports pending ECG and echo → louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
The innocent murmurs after infancy Still murmur: vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine · Pulmonic flow murmur: systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla · Venous hum: continuous, supra/infraclavicular, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with head flexion and when supine.
The continuous murmur A continuous murmur in a child has three causes, separated by location: Right infraclavicular and positional: venous hum, benign, fades with head flexion and when supine · Left infraclavicular and fixed: patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture; runs through S2, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure · Over the back with weak femoral pulses: coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension. Separately, a fixed split S2 is the atrial septal defect sign, so an S2 split that moves with respiration excludes atrial septal defect.
Pairs with Congenital Heart Disease covers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column. Heart Murmurs in an Adult covers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?"
The four innocent murmurs Still murmur: younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence · Pulmonic flow murmur: childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety · Venous hum: continuous, supra- or infraclavicular, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with head flexion · Peripheral pulmonary stenosis: the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; typical under 1 year · Persistence past the expected age: a benign murmur that outlives its window is itself a pathologic feature · Intensity and defect size: a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens
How NBME framed it A murmur new on day 3 after a normal birth examination pulls toward a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus; its soft grade and spread to the axilla mark peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The options were the five common acyanotic lesions, so the key was the umbrella term, pulmonary stenosis.
Transferable rule In screening, reassurance requires the entire benign profile. One pathologic feature on exam, in the vitals or in the history is sufficient to start the workup.
Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus: it is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle. Check the side and the positional change; a ductus murmur does not change with head position.
Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect: the split S2 here moves with respiration, the opposite of the fixed split it requires.
Mirror twinHypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it is the dangerous mimic of the innocent murmur; the direction the murmur moves on standing separates them.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance: accept it only after naming the full benign profile.
